claims.text: Ultra-rapid quenching combined with a brief sub-onset isothermal hold will suppress primary crystallization in Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
Ultra-rapid quenching combined with the hold will improve amorphous retention and thermal stability relative to slower cooling or uncontrolled reheating.
Melt-spinning can cool this alloy at approximately 10^5–10^6 K/s.
A hold near 900 K is below the primary crystallization onset and is suitable for avoiding crystallization.
The reported eutectic crystallization temperature under accelerated cooling is approximately 960 K.
The 960 K eutectic crystallization temperature is an applicable upper boundary for a post-quench isothermal hold.
A hold near 900 K is above the glass-transition temperature of this alloy.
Rapid cooling suppresses atomic diffusion and nucleation, thereby kinetically trapping an amorphous structure.
A brief sub-onset hold produces controlled structural relaxation that stabilizes the amorphous arrangement.
The isothermal hold relieves internal stresses without allowing crystal nuclei sufficient time to grow.
Adding the isothermal hold will retain more amorphous phase than rapid quenching alone.
Adding the hold will delay or shift crystallization events to higher temperatures during reheating.
Slow cooling of Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 produces a complex crystalline microstructure.
Rapid quenching of Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 yields an amorphous structure.
The rapidly quenched amorphous phase is thermally unstable and undergoes primary crystallization during reheating.
Cooling rates of at least 10^5 K/s are required for the proposed intervention to be effective.
A 900 K hold lasting 1–2 seconds is likely to provide an effective processing window.
Phosphorus and high mixing entropy enhance glass-forming ability in this alloy.
Under accelerated cooling, FCC crystallization shifts from 1706 K to 1341 K and eutectic crystallization shifts from 1206 K to 960 K.
